{{Short description|Axioms in computational complexity theory}}
In [[computational complexity theory]] the '''Blum axioms''' or '''Blum complexity axioms''' are [[axioms]]  that specify desirable properties of complexity measures on the set of [[computable function]]s. The axioms were first defined by [[Manuel Blum]] in 1967.<ref>{{Cite journal | last = Blum | first = Manuel | authorlink = Manuel Blum| title = A Machine-Independent Theory of the Complexity of Recursive Functions | doi = 10.1145/321386.321395 | journal = [[Journal of the ACM]]| volume = 14 | issue = 2 | pages = 322–336| year = 1967 | s2cid = 15710280 | url = http://port70.net/~nsz/articles/classic/blum_complexity_1976.pdf}}</ref>

Importantly, [[Blum's speedup theorem]] and the [[gap theorem]] hold for any complexity measure satisfying these axioms. The most well-known measures satisfying these axioms are those of time (i.e., running time) and space (i.e., memory usage).

== Definition ==
To begin, we list all [[partial computable functions]]. That is, we assign a computable [[Numbering_(computability_theory)|numbering]] of these functions: <math>\varphi_0, \varphi_1, \dots</math>. For example, we may specify a specific [[programming language]], then assign <math>\varphi_n</math> to be the [[shortlex|length-lexicographically]] ''n''-th syntactically valid program according to that. Two programs <math>\varphi_n, \varphi_m</math> may compute the exact same [[partial function]], but have different numberings. This allows us to distinguish their "complexity"

Abstractly, to say that we are measuring the "complexity" of program <math>\varphi_n</math> means finding a function <math>\Phi_n</math>, such that for any program input <math>x</math>, the complexity/cost of computing <math>\varphi_n</math> on that input is <math>\Phi_n(x)</math>. If program <math>\varphi_n</math> does not halt on <math>x</math>, then <math>\Phi_n(x)</math> should be undefined. Otherwise, <math>\Phi_n(x)</math> should be a definite [[natural number]]. This gives us the first axiom:

* The [[domain of a function|domains]] of <math>\varphi_i</math> and <math>\Phi_i</math> are identical.

Further, the complexity measure should be computable in some sense, for non-computable complexity measures are not interesting in practice. This gives us the second axiom:

* There is a program that, given any <math>i, x, c \in \N</math>, decides whether <math>\Phi_i(x) \leq c</math>. Note that if <math>\Phi_i(x)</math> is undefined, then by definition <math>\Phi_i(x) \leq c</math> is FALSE for all <math>c \in \N</math>. In other words, the set <math>\{(i,x,c) \in \mathbb{N}^3 \mid \Phi_i(x) = c\}</math> is [[computable set|computable]].

These are the '''Blum axioms'''. A '''Blum complexity measure''' is a pairing <math>(\varphi, \Phi)</math> that satisfies the Blum axioms.

Given a Blum complexity measure, and any total computable function <math>f</math>, we define <math>C[f]</math> to be the class of functions of '''complexity class''' bounded by <math>f</math>. That is, <math>C[f]</math> consists of total computable functions <math>\phi</math>, such that there exists some <math>\varphi_n</math>, such that <math>\forall x, \; \Phi_n(x) \leq f(x)</math>.

The definition of complexity class is sometimes loosened to <math>\bar C[f]</math>, the class of functions bounded by <math>f</math> for ''almost all'' inputs. That is, <math>\bar C[f]</math> consists of total computable functions <math>\phi</math>, such that there exists some <math>\varphi_n</math>, such that <math>\Phi_n(x) \leq f(x)</math> for all but finitely many <math>x</math>.

=== Examples ===
[[Time complexity]] is a Blum complexity measure. To decide whether <math>\Phi_i(x) \leq c</math>, simulate <math>\varphi_i(x)</math> for <math>c</math> steps. If the machine halts before <math>c</math> steps are done, then output TRUE, else output FALSE.

Similarly, [[space complexity]] (or any computable combination of time and space), is a Blum complexity measure.

<math>(\varphi, \varphi)</math> is ''not'' a complexity measure, since it fails the second axiom.

== Properties ==
Assume all statements begin with "For any Blum complexity measure <math>(\varphi, \Phi)</math>...".

There are arbitrarily difficult ways of computing any function: for any total computable <math>f</math>, and any partial computable <math>\phi</math>, there exists some <math>\varphi_n</math> such that <math>\phi = \varphi_n</math>, and for any <math>x</math>, if <math>\varphi_n(x)</math> is defined, then <math>\Phi_n(x) > f(x)</math>.<ref name=":0">{{Citation |last=Smith |first=Carl H. |authorlink = Carl Herbert Smith|chapter=Abstract Complexity Theory |date=1994 |title=A Recursive Introduction to the Theory of Computation |pages=68–90 |chapter-url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-1-4419-8501-9_4 |place=New York, NY |publisher=Springer New York |doi=10.1007/978-1-4419-8501-9_4 |isbn=978-1-4612-6420-0|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>{{Reference page|location=Thm. 3.18}}

There are functions that are arbitrarily high in complexity class: for any total computable <math>f</math>, there exists total computable functions not in <math>\bar C[f]</math>.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|location=Thm. 3.20}}

[[Blum's speedup theorem]].

[[Gap theorem]]: Given any total computable <math>g</math>, there exists a total computable function <math>f</math> such that <math>C[f] = C[g\circ f]</math>. 

The construction is constructive. That is, the proof of the theorem is simply a program that, given a program computing <math>f</math>, outputs a program computing <math>g</math>.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|location=Thm. 3.26}}

The [[Edward M. McCreight|McCreight]] and [[Albert R. Meyer|Meyer]] union theorem:<ref>{{Cite book |last1=McCreight |first1=E. M. |last2=Meyer |first2=A. R. |chapter=Classes of computable functions defined by bounds on computation: Preliminary Report |date=1969-05-05 |title=Proceedings of the first annual ACM symposium on Theory of computing - STOC '69 |chapter-url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/800169.805423 |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |pages=79–88 |doi=10.1145/800169.805423 |isbn=978-1-4503-7478-1|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> Let <math>f(n, x)</math> be a total computable function, such that for any <math>n\in \N</math>, <math>f(n+1, x) > f(n, x)</math> for all but finitely many <math>x</math>. Then there exists a total computable function <math>F</math> such that <math>C[F] = \bigcup_{n \in \N} C[f(n, \cdot)]</math>.

[[Compression theorem]]:<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|location=Thm. 3.28}} Let <math>g(x, n)</math> be a total computable function. There exists a total computable function <math>f</math> such that, for any <math>n \in \N</math>:

* If <math>\varphi_n(x)</math> is defined, then <math>\varphi_{f(n)}(x) < x</math>. This condition is used to avoid trivially stacking up complexity in the output size.
* For any program <math>m</math> such that <math>\varphi_m = \varphi_{f(n)}</math>, we have <math>\Phi_m(x) \geq \Phi_n(x)</math> for almost all <math>x</math>. This gives the universal lower bound.
* <math>\Phi_{f(n)}(x) \leq g(x, \Phi_n(x))</math> for almost all <math>x</math>. This gives the existential upper bound.

== Complexity classes ==

For a [[total computable function]] <math>f</math> [[complexity class]]es of computable functions can be defined as
:<math>C(f) := \{ \varphi_i \in \mathbf{P}^{(1)} \mid \forall x.\ \Phi_i(x) \leq f(x) \}</math>
:<math>C^0(f) := \{ h \in C(f) \mid \mathrm{codom}(h) \subseteq \{0,1\} \}</math>

<math>C(f)</math> is the set of all computable functions with a complexity less than <math>f</math>. <math>C^0(f)</math> is the set of all [[boolean-valued function]]s with a complexity less than <math>f</math>. If we consider those functions as [[indicator function]]s on sets, <math>C^0(f)</math> can be thought of as a complexity class of sets.
